text: Stored rice can also be damaged by mold (ផ្សិត), mainly from fungal genera the source names as Aspergillus and Penicillium. Mold growth is favored by excess or uneven grain moisture (some grains in a lot wetter than others), physical damage to kernels, elevated temperature and humidity in the storage area, and grain that has already picked up some insect damage. Beyond spoiling grain appearance and taste, some molds produce mycotoxins (សារធាតុពុលមីកូតុកស៊ីន) — toxic compounds that are heat-stable, meaning they are not destroyed by ordinary cooking, and that can pose real health risks to people and livestock if contaminated grain is eaten regularly. Because early mold and toxin contamination is not always visible or detectable by smell, prevention matters more than trying to fix it after the fact: dry grain thoroughly and as evenly as possible before storage rather than storing partially dried or unevenly dried lots; keep the storage space dry and reasonably ventilated; avoid mixing wet grain with already-dry stock; do not reuse old sacks or bins that previously held moldy or infested grain without cleaning them first; and inspect stored seed grain periodically for signs of mold before using it for planting. For seed specifically, the source mentions seed treatment (ការព្យាបាលគ្រាប់ពូជ / seed treatment) as a practical safeguard farmers can apply to help protect seed lots from fungal damage before they are planted. (Note: this entry summarizes the qualitative points on mold and mycotoxin risk from the source; it does not give specific fungicide/seed-treatment product names or dosages — check current, locally approved products and follow label instructions for any actual treatment applied.)
